headline: State desk: Massachusetts veterans bill, Kentucky tops 30,000
dek: Massachusetts senators back veterans' medical access without a doctor's note, Kentucky tops 30,000 patients and South Dakota doubles its edible limit.
key_points: The Massachusetts Senate voted 35-4 for a supplemental budget that would let veterans register as medical patients with VA paperwork instead of a clinician's certification; the House must agree to the changes.
Kentucky's medical programme passed 30,000 registered cardholders, with 27 dispensaries operating and 47 of 80 approved businesses open, Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman announced this week.
South Dakota raised its medical edible limit to 100 mg of THC per serving from 50 mg on 5 November, keeping the 500 mg package cap.
A filed Washington initiative would ban growing cannabis or hemp in residential zones and needs 308,911 valid signatures by 31 December to reach lawmakers.
body: In the days after the election, state capitals were back to the slower work of rules and budgets. The Massachusetts Senate moved to open medical cannabis to veterans without a doctor's recommendation, Kentucky's young medical market reached a new size, South Dakota rewrote its edible rules, and a citizen initiative in Washington took aim at patients who grow at home. Here is what changed and why it matters for operators.
## Massachusetts: veterans without the doctor's visit

On Thursday, 5 November, the Massachusetts Senate voted 35-4 for an amended supplemental budget that includes a significant change to the medical programme, Marijuana Moment reported. Veterans could register as medical patients by showing official Veterans Affairs documentation of a debilitating condition, and the Cannabis Control Commission would be barred from also requiring a clinician's certification.

The fix targets a real gap: VA doctors are still not allowed to fill in state medical marijuana recommendation forms, so veterans have had to pay for outside consultations. The Senate version also adds post-traumatic stress disorder, opioid use disorder and chronic pain to the list of qualifying conditions; Gov. Maura Healey's original filing did not include opioid use disorder.

For operators, medical status matters in Massachusetts because medical purchases are exempt from the sales, excise and local taxes charged on adult-use sales, and patients can buy more and stronger products. The bill now goes back to the House to reconcile differences before it can reach Healey. It comes days after voters rejected Question 8, the repeal of adult-use sales, by about 76% to 24%. A law enforcement reform group, LEAP, calculated that the repeal campaign's more than $3.7 million in spending, almost all from SAM Action, exceeded the annual public safety budgets of 124 of the 346 municipalities that reported data.

Kentucky's medical programme, which opened its first dispensary in December 2025, now has more than 30,000 registered cardholders, Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman announced, in a milestone reported by Marijuana Moment on 6 November. More than 500 practitioners are approved to recommend cannabis, 27 retailers are operating, including a new store in Maysville, and 47 of the 80 approved businesses are up and running.

The pace is notable. Our Kentucky hub recorded 12 dispensaries open as of May 2026; the count has more than doubled since. In October, Gov. Andy Beshear said dispensaries were open in all 11 licensing regions, and a June executive order added 15 qualifying conditions after lawmakers declined to expand the list. Patients may vaporize flower but not smoke it, and home growing is not allowed.
> Kentucky built a medical market from zero to 30,000 patients in under a year, and more than a third of its licensed businesses are still not open.

South Dakota's Department of Health raised the maximum THC in a single serving of a medical edible from 50 mg to 100 mg, effective 5 November, The Marijuana Herald reported. The 500 mg cap per package, child-resistant packaging and serving labels are unchanged, and tinctures, oils and capsules are outside the serving limit.

Regulators said the change fixes an inconsistency: packaging rules already allowed up to 100 mg per serving in some cases, while a manufacturing rule capped producers at 50 mg. The edible change is one part of a package amending 35 sections of the medical rules, covering testing, operations, security, registration and penalties. Sen. Taffy Howard questioned the increase at the 14 October rules committee hearing. About 19,800 patients were registered as of September, according to our South Dakota hub.
## Washington: an initiative against home grows

In Washington, Tukwila resident Regis Costello filed Initiative IL27-432 on 15 October. The attorney general's office issued its ballot title on 4 November. The measure would ban growing marijuana or hemp in residential zones and impose licensing and insurance requirements on certain cannabis and hemp activities.

Because Washington adults without a medical authorization already cannot grow at home, the ban would land mainly on patients: registered patients may grow six plants, up to 15 with a practitioner's approval, and unregistered patients with an authorization up to four. The ballot summary does not explain how the ban would interact with the medical law. Backers need 308,911 valid signatures by 31 December to send it to the 2027 Legislature, which could pass it, reject it or let it go to the November 2027 ballot. A similar measure was filed last year. Separately, a 2026 bill to let adults grow six plants has not become law.

In Massachusetts, whether the House accepts the Senate's veterans language in the final budget. In Kentucky, how quickly the remaining 33 approved businesses open. In Washington, whether the initiative's backers file enough signatures by 31 December. And in Michigan, as we noted on 7 November, the new excise-tax filing portal opens on 12 November.
